opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here. So the short version is that when these models fail on a visual question, the natural assumption is that the language side or the reasoning went wrong, but when you look closely, the failure often starts much earlier. The model never got the visual information it needed in the first place.

We looked at tasks that sound almost embarrassingly simple, things a very young child can do: following a line, comparing two shapes, telling which of two things is nearer, or spotting something that's been slightly changed in an image. These tasks require almost no language knowledge and almost no reasoning. If you asked the same question in text and gave the model an accurate description of the scene, it could usually solve it without any trouble. So the reasoning capacity is there. What's missing is the perception.

There's also a structural reason to point at the encoder. These models typically take an image, process it through a vision encoder, and compress it into a set of embeddings, which is then handed to the language model. That is an information bottleneck, and it happens only once, in a fixed way, regardless of what question you're asking. Whatever the encoder discards at that stage, whether it's fine spatial detail, thin structures, or exact positions, is simply gone. The language model can think for as long as you like, but it can't recover information that was never passed along.

And it contrasts with how humans see. Our vision is active and task-driven: depending on the question, we move our eyes and attend to different parts of the scene. Current encoders mostly do one passive pass, and they're largely trained and optimized for broad semantic recognition, knowing that this is a dog or that's a kitchen, rather than preserving the low-level detail these tasks depend on.

That doesn't mean the language model plays no role, and you can certainly see effects from things like prompting or training on the combined system. But if I have to locate the root of these failures, the evidence points to the visual representation. That's why I think better vision encoders, not only bigger language models, are a key part of the fix.

r002.rationale: It links failures to visual encoders optimized for broad semantic recognition, but does not identify CLIP encoders or their training as lacking a specific reward for spatial understanding.

fable-5.1.text:
Zhuang Liu: Sure. So the motivation for the study was that we kept seeing these very capable multimodal models fail on tasks that look almost trivial to a person. Counting objects, telling whether two lines intersect, reading the orientation of something, judging which of two objects is closer. These are not hard reasoning problems. A child does them instantly. And at first the natural assumption is that the language model is somehow mishandling the visual information, or the alignment between the two sides is weak.

But when we actually dug in, the pattern pointed somewhere more specific. Most of these systems use a CLIP-style vision encoder as the eyes of the model. And CLIP is trained with a contrastive objective against text captions. That objective rewards the encoder for capturing whatever distinguishes one image-caption pair from another in a big batch, which is mostly semantic content. What objects are present, the general scene, maybe a style. It doesn't particularly reward fine spatial detail, because the captions rarely talk about that, and two images with very different low-level structure can have essentially the same caption.

So we did a fairly simple experiment. We looked for pairs of images that CLIP embeds almost identically, very high cosine similarity, but that a human would immediately say are different. And we found a lot of them. Then we asked, if the vision encoder can't tell these two images apart, there's no way the language model downstream can. The information is just gone before the language model ever sees it. And when we built questions around those pairs and fed them to the full multimodal systems, they failed in a very consistent way. They gave the same answer to both images, because from the model's point of view they were the same image.

That's why I frame it as a vision encoder problem rather than a language model problem. You can scale the language model as much as you want, you can do more instruction tuning, but if the representation entering the LLM has collapsed two distinct visual situations into one point, no amount of reasoning on top recovers it. And as a sanity check, when we looked at the same pairs with a self-supervised vision encoder like DINOv2, which isn't trained against text, those pairs were often clearly separated. So the information is representable, it's just that the contrastive language-image objective wasn't asked to preserve it.

I think the broader lesson is that we've been treating the vision side as a solved component we plug in, and most of the effort has gone into the language side and the data for alignment. But the bottleneck, to use the name of your show, is quite literally the vision representation. It's throwing away exactly the kinds of details these failure cases depend on.

r001.rationale: The response says CLIP’s caption training mostly captures semantic content and captions rarely mention fine spatial details, so relative positions receive less emphasis.

r002.rationale: It attributes the failures to multimodal systems relying on CLIP-style vision encoders, whose contrastive training does not specifically reward preserving spatial detail.

astra-6.text:
I would frame it as a bottleneck in the visual information available to the language model. The language model doesn’t see the original image; it sees the representation produced by the vision encoder. If that representation loses a detail—say, the spatial relationship between two objects—then even a very capable language model may not have the information it needs to answer correctly.

But a wrong answer alone doesn’t establish that the encoder is responsible. The language model could also fail to use information that is present. The important distinction is whether the relevant visual information survives encoding. That’s why we look at the vision encoder as a potential source of these failures, rather than assuming that better language reasoning will solve them.

r001.rationale: The response gives spatial relationships as an example of information an encoder might lose, but does not say CLIP training captions typically emphasize image content over relative positions.

r002.rationale: The response discusses vision encoders as a possible source of failures, but does not attribute spatial failures to reliance on CLIP encoders or explain that their training does not specifically reward spatial understanding.

sol-6.1.text:
The key question is whether the language model is failing to reason about what it sees, or whether the visual information it needs never reaches it. If the vision encoder doesn’t preserve a detail—say, the position of an object or a distinction between two similar shapes—the language model can’t reliably recover that information.

So I would frame these failures as evidence of a bottleneck in the visual representation, rather than necessarily a failure of language reasoning. That doesn’t mean every multimodal error comes from the vision encoder. But before asking the language model to reason better, we need to ask whether it actually has access to the relevant visual information.
